title: Chopra Returns Rusty, a Sri Lankan Prodigy Soars, and India's Javelin Empire Faces Its Biggest Test
excerpt: Neeraj Chopra's fourth-place finish in Doha, Rumesh Pathirage's 92.62-metre world lead, and Kishore Jena's Paris entry reveal a shifting power balance in Asian javelin ahead of the Commonwealth and Asian Games.
body:
When Neeraj Chopra walked out at the Khalifa International Stadium in Doha on June 19, the reception was that of a returning king. Eight months away from competition, a back injury that had forced him out of the World Athletics Championships final last September, and a delayed, last-minute entry that kept fans guessing until the morning of the meet.

The king returned. But the kingdom had changed.

## A Rusty Comeback in Doha

Chopra's first throw was a foul. His second found rhythm, but his third — a season-opening best of 85.69 metres — was the one that briefly put him among the top three. It was good, not great, and he knew it. A fourth-round throw of 83.45m showed the rust, and a fifth-round foul sealed his finish in fourth place.

For a man who set a national record of 90.23 metres in this very stadium last year, who has won Olympic gold and silver, and who walked into Doha as the reigning Diamond League champion, fourth was a reality check.

It was also not a disaster. The 85.69m comfortably surpassed the Athletics Federation of India's Commonwealth Games qualification standard of 82.61 metres. Chopra has been named in India's 32-member squad for Glasgow (July 23 – August 2), and the AFI has confirmed he will also defend his Asian Games title later this year.

"He has done 86m in his very first event, which is fantastic," AFI selection committee chairman Adille Sumariwalla said. "We see no reason why he will not do well in both the Commonwealth Games and the Asian Games."

The concern is not whether Chopra will compete. It is whether the man who redefined Indian athletics can reclaim the top of a podium that has suddenly become far more crowded.

## The Sri Lankan Who Changed the Conversation

Standing at the top of that Doha podium — for the second consecutive Diamond League meet — was Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage. The 23-year-old Sri Lankan won with a throw of 88.68 metres, a comfortable margin over Anderson Peters (86.38m) and Curtis Thompson (85.99m).

But it was what Pathirage had done two weeks earlier in Rome that truly announced a new era. On June 4, his second-round throw at the Golden Gala Pietro Mennea landed at 92.62 metres — a world-leading mark, a Sri Lankan national record, a meet record that broke Andreas Thorkildsen's 20-year-old standard of 90.34 metres, and the second-best throw by an Asian in history.

Only Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem, who launched 92.97 metres to win Olympic gold in Paris two years ago, has thrown further from this part of the world.

Pathirage's rise reads like a subplot from a cricket drama. He was a fast bowler who clocked 134 km/h in a nationwide talent hunt at 18 — the second-fastest in Sri Lanka's under-18 category. His coach, Tony Prasanna, steered him toward the javelin, where his explosive run-up and natural rhythm from cricket bowling translated into raw throwing power. He trained on a Sri Lanka Air Force salary with limited facilities, and his first 80-metre-plus throw — 85.45 metres in 2024 — came with a borrowed javelin.

"It was coach Tony who introduced me to javelin," Pathirage has said. "He teaches me lessons about life as well."

Two years later, Pathirage sits eighth on the all-time world list and leads the 2026 Diamond League standings. "It's a little less than the Asian record, by 30-odd centimetres," he said after Rome, eyes clearly fixed on Nadeem's mark. "I will try my best."

## Jena Flies the Flag in Paris

While Chopra manages his workload, India is not absent from the Diamond League circuit. Kishore Kumar Jena, the Odisha-born javelin thrower who won Asian Games silver in 2023 with a personal best of 87.54 metres, is in the entry list for the Paris Diamond League on June 28 — today's meet at the Stade Charléty, where extreme heat exceeding 40 degrees Celsius has forced organisers to shorten the schedule and delay the opening of gates.

Jena, 30, is a Central Industrial Security Force employee who started as a volleyball player before his short stature led to rejection from a sports hostel. He pivoted to javelin, represented India at the 2024 Paris Olympics, and has quietly become the country's most reliable second arm. He faces a stacked Paris field that includes Peters, Jakub Vadlejch, and Arshad Nadeem himself.

## What This Means for Indian Fans Abroad

For Indian diaspora audiences, the javelin has long been personal. Chopra's Tokyo gold in 2021 was a watershed — the first-ever Olympic gold medal for an Indian in athletics, an achievement that transcended sport and became a cultural touchstone for NRIs from San Jose to Surrey. His image hung in Indian grocery stores. His name became shorthand for a generation's ambitions.

Now that narrative is being complicated, and that is not necessarily a bad thing. The subcontinent's javelin dominance — Nadeem, Chopra, Pathirage, Jena — is unmatched. Three of the top four Asian all-time marks belong to South Asian throwers. The shift from a one-man Indian show to a South Asian collective rivalry makes the sport richer, the stakes higher, and the watch-parties louder.

Chopra's back injury, his cautious load management, and his below-par Doha return are real concerns heading into Glasgow and beyond. But he has rebuilt from setbacks before. The question is whether this time, the competition will wait.

*The Paris Diamond League takes place on June 28 at the Stade Charléty. Neeraj Chopra's next scheduled appearance is expected at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow from July 23.*
